question: Have large langauge models been applied to the schema matching problem in databases and are they effective?

sections.title: Application of Zero-Shot LLMs
sections.text: Recent research has explored the utility of large language models in the domain of database schema matching. Specifically, studies by Sheetrit et al. and Zhang et al. have employed pre-trained large language models in a zero-shot setting to address this problem [1]. This approach leverages the inherent capabilities of these models to perform matching tasks without the need for task-specific fine-tuning or additional training data [1].

sections.title: Limitations in Large-Scale Environments
sections.text: Despite the potential of using large language models for schema matching, significant challenges arise when scaling these methods to larger database environments. While the zero-shot prompting strategies that involve providing entire schemas to the model have shown effectiveness on small databases, this approach fails when applied to larger datasets [2]. The inability to handle the increased complexity and volume of data in large-scale databases represents a critical limitation for current LLM-based schema matching techniques [2].

sections.title: Alternative Approaches for Schema Linking
sections.text: To address the inefficiencies and failures associated with direct LLM prompting on large databases, alternative methodologies have been proposed for related tasks such as text-to-SQL generation. One such approach is schemagraphsql, which focuses on efficient schema linking [3]. This method utilizes pathfinding graph algorithms to navigate and link schemas, offering a more robust solution for large-scale databases where traditional LLM prompting struggles [3]. By shifting the focus from direct language model inference to algorithmic graph traversal, these methods aim to overcome the scalability barriers identified in previous LLM applications [3].

question: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) receivers can provide a reference clock signal known as Pulse-per-Second (PPS or 1-PPS). Is the PPS physically generated through a digitally-controlled oscillator (or line driver) whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the estimated clock bias (retrieved by means of PVT algorithms)?

sections.title: Timestamping and Measurement Reference
sections.text: The primary utility of the 1PPS signal in embedded systems is its function as a precise temporal reference for data acquisition. Microcontrollers within sensor nodes utilize this signal to timestamp measurements relative to the start of a whole second [2]. This capability allows for the synchronization of local data with a global time standard, which is critical for applications requiring high-precision timing across distributed networks [2]. The use of the 1PPS edge as a trigger ensures that measurement records are aligned with the second boundary defined by the GNSS receiver [2].
